functional.text: Several users edit the same document concurrently; everyone converges to the same text.
Edits from other collaborators appear in real time.
Version history: browse and restore earlier revisions.
Presence: see who is in the document and their cursors and selections.
Short offline periods: keep typing, sync on reconnect.

non_functional.text: Low latency: others see an edit within ~200 ms p99 in-region; local typing never waits on the network.
Convergence: all copies end identical and keep each user's intent.
Durability: an acknowledged edit is never lost.
Availability 99.95%; a server crash interrupts a session for seconds only.

assumptions.text: 1B documents, ~50 KB each; ~20M connected users at peak, ~5M typing at once, ~1 batched op per second each.
Most documents have 1–2 editors; at most ~100 concurrent editors per document (more as viewers).

out_of_scope.text: Spreadsheets/slides, comments and suggestions, full-text search, multi-region active-active editing of one doc.

api.notes: Creates metadata, ACL and an empty snapshot.
Latest snapshot plus the op-log tail, folded on the server.
One socket per open document; ops are batched every ~100–200 ms.
History view; restore = a new op that sets the old state.

data.name: op_log
data.fields: doc_id (partition), rev (clustering), op (insert/delete/format + position), author, client_seq, ts
data.why: Append-only, ~100 B per op, read by doc in rev order; client_seq makes resends idempotent.

data.name: snapshots
data.why: Every ~500 ops; open = latest snapshot + tail.

data.name: docs
data.fields: doc_id, title, owner, acl[(user, role)], created_at, last_rev
data.why: Small relational data; lists and sharing queries.

parts.title: Real-time session and transport
parts.problem: Deliver every edit to all other editors of the same document within ~200 ms, for ~20M connected users, and give each document one place where its edits are put in order.

options.name: HTTP polling every second
options.cons: up to 1 s delay; 20M requests/s mostly empty; ordering still needs a single place

options.name: SSE down + HTTP POST up
options.pros: simple server push; proxies like it
options.cons: two channels to keep in order; one request per edit batch

options.name: WebSocket to the server that owns the document (route by doc_id, ownership lease)
options.pros: one ordered, full-duplex channel; doc state in one server's memory
options.cons: stateful servers: routing, leases and failover to design

options.name: peer-to-peer (WebRTC) between editors
options.cons: NAT traversal, no central order or persistence, breaks with 100 editors

parts.choice: WebSocket per editor, routed by doc_id to a collaboration server that holds an ownership lease for that document
parts.why: N1 needs push, and ordering is far simpler when one process owns a document. At ~50k sockets per server, 20M connections need ~400 servers. A single doc peaks at ~500 ops/s (100 editors), which one process handles easily. The lease in etcd guarantees one owner even during failover.

nodes.label: L7 load balancer (WebSocket, route by doc_id)

parts.title: Concurrency control: OT vs CRDT
parts.problem: Two people type at the same position at the same time, each on a local copy. Every copy must end up identical, and each person's intent (where their text went) must be kept.

options.name: lock a paragraph while someone edits it
options.cons: people wait on each other; stuck locks; not real co-editing

options.name: last write wins on the whole document
Operational Transformation with a central server
options.pros: server assigns revisions and transforms each op against the ops it missed; compact ops; mature for rich text
options.cons: needs a central orderer; transform functions are subtle; long offline periods mean big transforms

options.name: CRDT (sequence CRDT with unique ids per character)
options.pros: merges in any order without a server; great offline and P2P
options.cons: per-character ids and tombstones grow the document; rich-text intent is harder

parts.choice: Operational Transformation, ordered by the document's owner server; clients send one batch at a time and wait for its ack
parts.why: P1 already gives each document a single owner, which is exactly what OT needs, and it keeps the stored document compact. Sending one outstanding batch per client means the server only transforms against ops since the client's base revision. A CRDT is the better answer if offline-first or P2P were requirements; here offline is short (F5).

nodes.label: L7 load balancer (WebSocket, route by doc_id)

parts.title: Persistence: op log and snapshots
parts.problem: Never lose an acknowledged edit, keep full revision history, and still open a document with a long history quickly.

options.name: save the whole document on every change
options.cons: 50 KB per edit × 5M edits/s ≈ 250 GB/s of writes; no history

options.name: append each op to a log, with no snapshots
options.cons: opening an old document replays a million ops

options.name: append each op to a log before acking; snapshot asynchronously every ~500 ops
options.pros: tiny durable writes; history = log; open = latest snapshot + short tail
options.cons: two stores to keep consistent; snapshot jobs to run

parts.choice: Op log (doc_id, rev) appended before the ack, plus asynchronous snapshots every ~500 ops
parts.why: An op is ~100 B, so 5M ops/s is ~0.5 GB/s of appends, cheap for a wide-column store partitioned by doc_id. Acking only after the append satisfies N3. Snapshots bound the replay on open and serve the history view; the snapshotter consumes a stream, so it never slows typing.

parts.title: Presence and cursors
parts.problem: Show who is in the document and where each person's cursor and selection are, updating smoothly, without turning every mouse move into a database write.

options.name: persist cursor positions in the database
options.cons: a write per keystroke for data nobody needs after they leave

options.name: Redis pub/sub shared by all servers
options.pros: works when editors of one doc sit on different servers
options.cons: an extra hop and a moving part we don't need: one server owns each doc

options.name: ephemeral state in the owner server's memory, broadcast at ≤ 10 Hz
options.pros: no storage at all; same channel as ops

parts.choice: Ephemeral presence in the owning collaboration server's memory, throttled to ≤ 10 updates/s per user, cursor positions transformed like ops
parts.why: Presence is soft state: it is worthless a few seconds later, so persistence is waste. Since every editor of a document is on the same server (P1), broadcasting is a local loop. Cursors must be transformed by concurrent ops, or they jump to the wrong place.

nodes.label: L7 load balancer (WebSocket, route by doc_id)

deep_dives.title: Owner server crash and failover

options.name: hot standby replicating the doc in memory
options.cons: doubles memory and fan-out for millions of mostly idle docs

options.name: lease expires; any server takes ownership and rebuilds from snapshot + op-log tail
options.pros: no standby cost; the log is already the source of truth
options.cons: a few seconds of reconnect for that doc's editors

deep_dives.choice: Lease-based takeover: the lease (~5 s TTL) expires, a new owner loads the latest snapshot plus the op-log tail, and clients reconnect with their last acked rev
deep_dives.why: Ops are acked only after the log append, so the log holds everything acknowledged (N3). The lease plus a fencing token (the lease revision) stops a paused old owner from appending, so two owners can never order the same document.

deep_dives.title: Reconnect and short offline periods

options.name: keep pending ops and the last acked rev; on reconnect fetch ops since rev, transform pending ops, resend
options.cons: very long offline periods mean large transforms

deep_dives.choice: Client keeps pending ops + last acked rev; on reconnect the server sends ops since that rev, the client transforms its pending ops and resends them (idempotent by client_seq)
deep_dives.why: F5 is about short gaps, which OT handles well. client_seq makes a resend after a lost ack harmless. Beyond a cap (e.g. 24 h or 10k ops) the client offers to save its version as a copy.

wrapup.bottlenecks: Very popular documents (100 editors, thousands of viewers) on one owner: move viewers to read-only fan-out replicas fed by the op stream. Op-log hot partitions per doc are fine at ~500 ops/s. Reconnect storms after a server dies: jittered backoff.
wrapup.failures: Owner crash: lease expires, a new owner rebuilds from snapshot + log, clients reconnect and resend pending ops. Op-log write fails: no ack, the client retries. Snapshotter down: opens get slower (longer tail), no data loss. Network drop: offline buffer and catch-up by rev.
wrapup.monitoring: Edit propagation latency (p50/p99 from send to peers' receipt), ack latency, transform error/conflict rate, ops per doc, sockets per server, lease takeovers, op-log append latency, snapshot lag (ops since last snapshot).
wrapup.scale: More collaboration servers: docs spread by consistent hashing on doc_id, and leases move with them. Op log scales by doc_id partitions. Viewers go to read-only replicas. ~400 servers at 20M sockets.
wrapup.future: Comments and suggestions as a separate op type, offline-first with a CRDT, multi-region with a per-doc home region, rich embeds.
